title: The Lakshmi who stays
hook: Indra lets a sage's garland be trampled and fortune leaves the worlds; the Sri Sukta asks for the Lakshmi who does not go away
carry: Lakshmi stays where she is honored

segments.voice: Yesterday: Agni carries the offering; the lamp invites her. Fire is the go-between. Today, why the gods needed her back at all.

A sage hands the king of the gods a garland. Indra, riding his great white elephant, drops it onto the elephant's head, and the elephant flings it to the ground and tramples it. In the Vishnu Purana, the sage, Durvasa, is furious: because you scorned this, he says, your fortune will leave you. And it does. Sri walks out of the three worlds. Plants wither. Nothing shines. That's why the gods had to churn the ocean, the story this week began with: to bring her back.
screen: `A GARLAND, TRAMPLED.` → `SRI LEAVES THE THREE WORLDS.` → `CHURN THE OCEAN, BRING HER BACK.`

segments.voice: When Lakshmi rose again, the Vishnu Purana says, Indra praised her with a hymn and asked for one thing: never leave the three worlds again. She agreed. The Sri Sukta asks the same, in its own words. In paraphrase: bring me, Jatavedas, that Lakshmi who does not go away, in whom I may find gold, cattle, horses and people. One long word: anapagamini, the one who does not go away. You only ask for someone who stays if you know what it is when someone leaves. Tradition calls Lakshmi restless. Here's the teaching, as many Hindus understand it: Lakshmi stays where she is honored. Indra lost her not by being poor but by treating a gift as nothing. That's why so many Hindu homes treat fortune like a guest. If a foot touches money or a book, a child is taught to touch it and bring the hand to the forehead, a small sorry. A first paycheck is often set before the family shrine, or offered to elders, before a rupee or a dollar is spent. And look at the hymn's list: gold, cattle, horses, and last, people. The faces around the table are counted among the riches. Today: a paycheck lands Friday and is gone by Thursday. The Sri Sukta doesn't promise more of it. It asks for the fortune with roots, and the story says how she's kept: with respect, not grabbing. A week behind us: the watcher, the goddess who is Brahman, two who are never apart, the voice in every word, and Lakshmi, rising, invited by fire, asked to stay.
screen: `INDRA ASKS: NEVER LEAVE AGAIN.` · `THE ONE WHO DOES NOT GO AWAY.` · `SHE STAYS WHERE SHE IS HONORED.` · `GOLD, CATTLE, HORSES, PEOPLE.` · then, large: `COME, AND DON'T GO.`

segments.voice: Notice the breath first: it leaves, and it comes back, without being asked. Then bring to mind one good thing in your life that hasn't gone away, a friend who keeps answering, a kitchen, a song that's still there, and rest with it, letting the thanks be quiet. If you pray, you can name it before Lakshmi or before God, in the words you already use; if you don't, let the steady thing be enough.
The Sri Sukta. The hymn to Sri, called Lakshmi, which asks the fire to bring her, and asks for the one who does not go away.
Your line: Lakshmi stays where she is honored. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: The Sri Sukta is chanted by some Hindus in Lakshmi worship at home and in temples, including at Diwali, and some families recite it on Fridays.

Jatavedas.meaning: a name of Agni, the fire

anapagamini.meaning: the one who does not go away

Lakshmi.meaning: the goddess of fortune, also called Sri

Durvasa.meaning: a sage famous for his quick temper

notes: Review and teach now pick up 1091 (the fire as go-between, avaha) and 1090 (gold, silver, moonlight); the two-readings (plain need vs inner) angle used on 1090 was replaced here with the honesty of asking for one who stays.

Verse 2 paraphrased: tāṃ ma āvaha jātavedo lakṣmīm anapagāminīm / yasyāṃ hiraṇyaṃ vindeyaṃ gām aśvaṃ puruṣān aham. Rendering puruṣān as 'people' (some translate 'men', 'servants', 'sons'); the script says 'some readers hear family, others helpers and guests'. Confirm.
